mainEntity.name: Is two weeks a standard waiting period after root canal, or does it vary?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two weeks is a commonly used interval, but the appropriate waiting time can vary depending on the clinical situation. Some cases may require a longer observation period — for example, if there was significant periapical infection, or if symptoms haven't fully resolved. Your dentist will assess your individual circumstances and advise accordingly. The priority is ensuring that the tooth is in a stable, settled condition before committing to a permanent crown, rather than adhering rigidly to a fixed timeframe in all cases.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat normally with a temporary filling after root canal treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can generally eat soft foods with care during the waiting period, but it's sensible to avoid chewing hard, chewy, or sticky foods on the side of the treated tooth. Hard foods could dislodge or crack the temporary restoration, and sticky foods may pull it out. If the temporary filling becomes loose or falls out, contact your dental practice promptly, as the tooth needs to remain protected to avoid bacterial contamination of the root canal system before the permanent crown is placed.

mainEntity.name: Will the tooth feel different or sensitive during the two-week wait?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's quite common to experience some degree of mild tenderness or sensitivity around the treated tooth in the days following root canal treatment. This typically relates to post-procedural tissue response rather than treatment failure, and it usually settles within a week or so. However, if your symptoms are severe, getting worse rather than better, or accompanied by swelling, you should contact your dentist for an assessment rather than waiting for your scheduled crown appointment.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I delay getting the crown after the two-week waiting period?

acceptedAnswer.text: Once your dentist has confirmed the tooth is ready for a crown, it's advisable not to delay the final restoration unnecessarily. A tooth that has undergone root canal treatment is structurally weakened and more susceptible to fracture without the protection of a permanent crown. A temporary filling is not designed as a long-term solution. Prolonged delay increases the risk of the tooth fracturing, the temporary restoration failing, or bacterial re-contamination of the root canal system — all of which can complicate or compromise the outcome of treatment.

mainEntity.name: Does a root canal always require a crown afterwards?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always — though a crown is the most commonly recommended option for back teeth (premolars and molars) following root canal treatment because they endure significant biting forces. For front teeth, which experience less pressure, a crown may not always be necessary, and other restorations such as a composite filling may be considered clinically appropriate. The decision depends on the individual tooth, the extent of existing damage or decay, and the clinical assessment of your dentist.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my root canal treatment has been successful?

acceptedAnswer.text: Signs that root canal treatment has been successful typically include the gradual resolution of pain and sensitivity over the weeks following the procedure, the absence of swelling or discharge around the treated tooth, and normal biting function. Your dentist may take follow-up X-rays at future appointments to monitor the periapical tissues for evidence of healing. It's important to attend these follow-up appointments as advised, as long-term radiographic monitoring is considered good clinical practice following endodontic treatment.
